content.text: A component re-renders when its own state changes, when an ancestor re-renders, or when a context it reads gets a new value. Changed props are not a trigger of their own: props change only because the parent rendered, and by default the child renders with it whether its props changed or not.

The support team reports that typing in the chat box feels sluggish. The React DevTools Profiler points at
, which draws a few hundred messages and renders again on every keystroke. The developer is puzzled:
, and it's the same array the whole time. "Its props didn't change, so why is it rendering?" The question has the model backwards, and fixing the model fixes the lag.
The belief goes like this: a component is a function of its props, so React re-renders it only when its props change. Same props, no render.
It's a reasonable thing to believe. Most of us learned React as "the UI is a function of props and state", which sounds like React checks the inputs before calling the function.

really does work that way, so it's easy to assume it's the default. And it's half true: a child that receives new props has indeed just rendered. The mistake is the direction of cause and effect. The new props didn't cause that render; the parent's render did, and it would have rendered the child with the old props too.

React's docs list two reasons for a render: the initial render, and a state update in the component or in one of its ancestors. Context adds a third path. Props aren't on the list. The previous article in this path covered what a render does; this one is about what starts one.
Trigger 1: the component's own state changes

schedules a render of that component. State inside a custom Hook counts too: it's still state of the component that calls the Hook. There is one shortcut. If the new value is identical to the current one under
, React skips re-rendering the component and its children. It may still call your component once before bailing out, but it throws that result away.
When a component renders, React renders every component it returns, recursively, without comparing props first. The
docs put it plainly: React normally re-renders a component whenever its parent re-renders. In the chat room, each keystroke updates

That's all "props changed" ever means. A component gets new props only when its parent renders, and when its parent renders, the child renders anyway. Props are a consequence of the trigger, never the trigger itself.

If an extra render breaks something, like a duplicated request or a counter that drifts, the bug is in the component, not in the render count. Render must be safe to repeat; a later article in this path covers why.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find the component that actually changed

content.text: Record the slow interaction in the React DevTools Profiler. For each component that rendered, walk up the tree to the nearest one whose state or context changed: that's the trigger, and everything below it rendered along with it.

items.title: Move state down to where it's read

content.text: If one small part of a big component reads a piece of state, extract that part and give it the state. Drafts, hover flags and open/closed toggles rarely belong at the top of a page.
